content: Echinacea plant preparations, belonging to the family Asteraceae, are commonly used in Europe and North America for the prevention and treatment of the common cold. However, the composition of Echinacea products varies significantly due to differences in plant material, extraction methods, and the addition of other components. This variability is often not well understood by consumers or physicians. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether Echinacea preparations are effective and safe compared to placebo for preventing and treating the common cold. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and sources was conducted, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, AMED, LILACS, Web of Science, CAMBASE, and others, up to June 2013. Experts in the field were also consulted to identify both published and unpublished studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared mono-preparations of Echinacea with placebo. Data from the included studies were independently assessed by at least two reviewers for eligibility, trial quality, and data extraction. The primary efficacy outcomes were the number of individuals experiencing at least one cold in prevention trials and the duration of colds in treatment trials. Safety and acceptability were assessed by examining the number of participants who dropped out due to adverse events. Trial quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of bias tool. A total of 24 double-blind trials involving 4631 participants and 33 comparisons between Echinacea preparations and placebo met the inclusion criteria. These trials used a variety of Echinacea preparations derived from different species and plant parts. Seven trials specifically investigated preparations based on the aerial parts of Echinacea purpurea. Of the included trials, ten were judged to have a low risk of bias, six had an unclear risk of bias, and eight had a high risk of bias. Ten trials (with 13 comparisons) focused on prevention, while 15 trials (with 20 comparisons) investigated treatment. One trial addressed both prevention and treatment. Due to significant clinical heterogeneity among the studies, the main analysis did not involve pooling of results. None of the 12 prevention comparisons that reported the number of patients with at least one cold episode found a statistically significant difference between Echinacea and placebo. However, a post hoc pooling of these results suggested a relative risk reduction of 10% to 20%. Among the six treatment trials that reported data on the duration of colds, only two demonstrated a significant effect of Echinacea over placebo. The number of participants who dropped out or reported adverse effects did not differ significantly between the treatment and control groups in either prevention or treatment trials. However, in prevention trials, there was a trend toward a higher number of participants dropping out due to adverse events in the Echinacea treatment groups. In conclusion, Echinacea products have not been shown to provide clear benefits for treating the common cold. While some individual prophylaxis trials showed positive trends, these effects were not statistically significant and are of questionable clinical relevance. It is possible that certain Echinacea products may offer a weak benefit, but the evidence remains inconclusive.
